# Two hand-maintained copies of a security-relevant rule need one source of
# truth for what they must agree on, or "the two are checked against the same
# corpus" is a claim rather than a fact.
# These define the *stack-line* rule -- StackFrames.parse, and the parseFrame
# that mirrors it in the browser. That is the rule applied to each line of an
# error's stack, and it is the only place a frame can be told apart from the
# continuation line of a multi-line message, because only the browser ever
# sees the stack. A `drop` here therefore means "this is not a stack line",
# not "this string can never be published": several of the drops are shaped
# like locations, and a payload that sends one directly as a bare `frame` or
# `source` is trusted no more and no less than any other location.
# Format: <verdict> TAB <text> TAB <expected location, for keep and loc>
#   keep  a stack line naming a location; the third column is the location the
#         filter must return, without the function name that preceded it.
#         StackFrames.parse and the browser's parseFrame must both give it,
#   loc   not a stack line, but a valid location on its own -- which is what
#         the collector actually sends in `frame`. parse must refuse it (it is
#         not a frame) and frame must return it unchanged. These rows are what
#         exercise frame's location-first branch; without them the frame loop
#         merely repeats the parse loop, which is how a scoped path came to be
#         mangled and a whole stack line came to be published raw, both with a
#   drop  neither. Nothing may come out of it through any entry point.
# Lines starting with # are comments; blank lines are ignored. No line may
# contain a tab of its own.
# Paths with an @ in them. The rule is that an @ after a slash is part of the
# path and never a name separator, so these have to survive whole: a scoped
# npm package -- most of the component library lives under one -- and the
# virtual paths a dev server serves. Getting this wrong mangles a large share
# of real insights rather than a crafted case.
# Version-pinned CDN and import-map URLs. The @ before the version follows a
# letter, not a slash, so a rule keyed on the previous character rejected all
# of these -- and an app served from jsDelivr, unpkg or esm.sh lost `frame` and
# `source` for every browser error. What marks a path is that its prefix is
# rooted or schemed, which these are and a function name is not.
# Firefox names a nested function outer/inner and an anonymous one outer/<, so
# a name may contain a slash. "The prefix contains a slash" would read these as
# paths and publish the name glued to the location; "rooted or schemed" does
# Shapes the previous, name-validating rule dropped. They cost nothing now:
# the name is not examined at all.
# A path segment or host need not be ASCII, and a Windows path and a bundler's
# virtual path carry characters a URL does not.
# Firefox names no function for a top-level frame, so the @ has nothing in
# A script URL carrying credentials. Refused by a rule of its own -- an @
# inside the authority, with something in front of it -- rather than by the
# path rule, since a version pin and a password share nothing but the
# character. No loss worth keeping: browsers do not load subresources from
# userinfo URLs, and a location with a password in it is the last thing that
# should travel in a forwarded payload.
# --- the price of having no rule about names ----------------------------
# The @ form has no delimiter, so the line as a whole has to look like a frame
# line before its @ counts as a separator: no whitespace anywhere, and both a
# line and a column. That is what keeps a sentence containing an @ from being
# split into a "name" and something that passes for a location -- and since
# the first line that parses wins and a message precedes the stack, such a
# line would displace the real frame, not just add a host.
# It costs these, which are real: Safari's pseudo-names and Firefox's
# space-containing async markers. firstFrame moves to the next line, and where
# one of these is the only line in the stack the insight falls back to
# `source`, which the browser supplies for a top-level script error. The
# alternative was an allowlist of engine-generated names, and four rounds of
# rules about what may stand in front of the @ was enough.

# Not stack lines, so parse refuses them; frame has to hand them back whole.
# A hashed bundle name: digits in the file are not evidence of anything, so

# A port is not a line number.
# Every @ follows a slash, so none of these is a name glued to a path.

# location on one side and not the other.

# A line number is a position in a file. Both forms matter: appending a column
# was all it took to slide the over-long run back into the "file", which FILE
